conceptTag: A small supplier vs a giant retailer
readerTitle: When the giant buyer sends a list of demands
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소형 식품용기 제조사와 대형 유통 체인, 소형 소프트웨어 회사와 대형 유통사 구매팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 작은 쪽이 협상에서 쓸 수 있는 힘은 버티기가 아니라, 준비된 대안과 여러 조건을 묶어 맞바꾸는 데서 나온다.
misconception: 거대 고객 앞에서 작은 공급자는 요구를 받아들이거나 거절하는 것 말고는 선택지가 없다.

sources.text: 협상의 표준 개념 (BATNA, 다중 이슈 맞교환)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 결제 기한 계산: 월 매입 $150,000, 30일→90일로 60일 연장 = 약 2개월치 매출 = 약 $300,000이 추가로 묶임.
대형 유통사의 공급자 거래 관행(결제 기한, 판촉비 분담 등)을 규제하는 법은 나라마다 다릅니다. 레슨에서는 법률 조언을 하지 않고 일반적인 협상 원리만 다뤘습니다.

cards.title: When the giant buyer sends a list of demands
body: Mira runs a 40-person factory that makes glass food containers. A national retail chain is her biggest customer.
On Monday the chain's buyer emails: cut prices 8%, move payment from 30 days to 90, and help pay for in-store promotions. "Please confirm by Friday."
The chain is a giant. Mira's company is not. She still has more options than it looks.

image.label: A small factory owner reading a long email from a huge store
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 공장 사무실에서 사장이 노트북을 보고 있고, 화면 뒤로 거대한 마트 건물이 그림자처럼 드리움. 이메일 화면에 요구 사항 세 줄. 실제 유통사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Mira do before Friday?

options.text: Accept all three to protect the account
options.feedback: She keeps the customer today but gives away price, cash and promotion money for nothing in return. The buyer also learns that her first answer is always yes.

options.text: Offer to meet halfway on price, 4% instead of 8%
options.feedback: It sounds fair, but it treats the deal as one issue. She'd still face the 90-day terms and promotion costs, with nothing left to trade.

options.text: Map every issue, check her real alternatives, then ask what's driving the request
options.feedback: This uses **negotiating from a weak position** (know your fallback) and **many issues at once** (see what can be traded). It costs a few days and gains her room to move.

cards.title: Three demands hide more issues.
body: Mira lists what the deal really covers. Some items matter a lot to her and little to the chain. Others are the reverse. That gap is where **trades** come from.

breakdown.label: Price
breakdown.detail: About $144,000 a year on $1.8M of sales

cards.title: Her power is outside the room.
body: The chain doesn't need Mira's company. But it does need a reliable supplier for a product its shoppers buy every week. Switching suppliers takes time and carries risk.

Mira's own fallback matters more. Before replying, she calls two regional grocers and checks her online store's growth. She sets a **walk-away point**: the worst deal she'd accept before shifting effort elsewhere.
She doesn't need a better alternative than the chain. She needs one good enough that she isn't forced to say yes.

image.label: A scale tipped by small weights labeled with alternatives
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 한쪽에는 거대한 마트 블록, 다른 쪽에는 작은 공장 블록과 함께 작은 추 세 개("Regional grocers", "Online store", "Walk-away point"). 저울이 거의 수평에 가까워짐. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The buyer says the price cut is non-negotiable.
body: On the call, Mira learns the buyer has a target: lower cost per unit this year. Payment terms and promotions are "standard asks." Which counter fits best?

options.text: "We can do 5% if we keep 30-day terms and get a 12-month volume forecast."
options.feedback: She gives on the issue the buyer cares about most and protects her cash. That's **many issues at once**: trade, don't just give.

options.text: "We'll do the full 8%, but we need 60-day terms."
options.feedback: Better than accepting everything, but she pays the full price cut and still lends the chain a month of cash.

options.text: "No price change. Our costs went up too."
options.feedback: Firm, but from a **weak position** a flat no can end the talk. It also ignores that the buyer has a real target to hit.

cards.title: Payment terms can cost more than price.
body: The chain buys about $150,000 a month. Moving from 30 to 90 days means about two extra months of sales sit unpaid. That's roughly **$300,000** of Mira's cash, stuck in the chain's bank account.

For a small factory, that could mean a new loan or a delayed machine. For the chain, it's a minor line in a big budget. An issue worth a lot to one side and little to the other is the best thing to trade.

image.label: Two cash piles: a small price cut vs. a large sum tied up
image.brief: 막대 두 개 비교. "5% price cut: $90,000 a year"와 "60 extra days unpaid: about $300,000 tied up". 두 번째 막대를 강조색으로. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Trades don't fix dependence.
body: Good trading helps you win a round. If one customer is most of your sales, every round starts weak. The lasting fix is growing other customers between negotiations.
Don't invent alternatives either. Buyers talk, and a bluff that gets called costs you trust for years.
Finally, rules on how big retailers treat suppliers differ by country. Check local rules with an adviser, not a negotiation lesson.

cards.title: Now you sell software to the giant.
body: Your 12-person company sells a stock-forecasting tool. A big retailer wants it in 300 stores. Procurement asks for 30% off, unlimited users and three custom features. What's your reply?

options.text: Accept. A famous name on your client list is worth it
options.feedback: You land the logo but may lose money serving it, and custom features can eat your small team's roadmap for a year.

options.text: Offer the discount for a three-year deal, a phased rollout and a public case study, with custom work priced separately
options.feedback: You give on price and get commitment, proof and protected engineering time. That's **many issues at once**, backed by a clear walk-away point from **weak position** thinking.

options.text: Hold your list price and say you treat every customer the same
options.feedback: It protects your pricing, but it leaves value on the table. A long contract or case study could be worth more to you than the discount costs.

cards.title: Small doesn't mean stuck. Prepare your fallback, then trade.
list: **Negotiating from a weak position:** build real alternatives and set a walk-away point before you answer
**Many issues at once:** list every term, then trade what's cheap for you for what's costly for you
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list every term in your biggest customer's contract. Mark which ones matter most to you and which matter most to them.
